clue.text: Clinton perhaps fears following old amendments to US Constitution

indicators.note: says the fears come after the old, so the letters for 'fears' go after O

parts.note: Bill Clinton, the US president, gives his first name as an example
frights are fears or scares

explanation.surface: A former president, scared, follows some antiquated changes to the American constitution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts FRIGHTS after O. 'Clinton perhaps' looks like a person in the surface but just gives a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bill of Rights is the collective name for the first ten amendments added to the US Constitution in 1791.

clue.text: Fool lover with nothing on

parts.note: a buff is an enthusiast or lover of something, as in a film buff
O, the figure zero, stands for nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A silly romantic is pictured wearing no clothes at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the buff' means naked, which the surface plays on, but here BUFF is an enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffoon is a clown or ridiculous person, a synonym for a fool.

clue.text: John almost set free

parts.note: john is American slang for a lavatory, as is the British loo

indicators.note: almost means the word set loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A man called John has nearly been released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' removes the last letter of SET, leaving SE. John is not a name here but a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose and free are synonyms as verbs: to loose an animal is to release it.

clue.text: Faded blue

definitions.meaning: ... also means risque or smutty, like a blue joke

explanation.surface: A description of a garment whose blue dye has washed out.
explanation.definitionFit: Off colour covers both senses: looking pale or poorly, and slightly indecent humour.

clue.text: King dismissed crushing defeat

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for king, from Latin rex
a batsman dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: A monarch was deposed after a heavy military loss.
explanation.definitionFit: A rout is a decisive defeat in which the losing side flees in disorder.

clue.text: Artful tug worried no female husky

indicators.note: worried means pulled about or shaken, so the remaining letters are rearranged
no female means the letter for female is struck out of the fodder

parts.note: anagram fodder once one letter is gone

explanation.surface: A crafty little pull, fretted over, with no woman involved, said in a hoarse voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' removes F from ARTFULTUG, and 'worried' rearranges the rest. 'husky' looks like a dog but describes a voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A guttural voice is throaty and rasping, much like a husky one.

clue.text: Ignoring the odds, it seems poor rate

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered letters leaves only the second, fourth and so on of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A gambler is advised that a poor rate makes betting look unwise.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is the speed or pace of something, so it means rate.

clue.text: Told education supports where pupils should be?

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits beneath, so ED goes after the other part

parts.note: pupils belong in a form, a school class, so they should be in form

explanation.surface: Someone was told that schooling props up where students belong.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a British school class or year group, so pupils should be IN FORM.
explanation.definitionFit: To be informed is to have been told something, so the past participle fits.

clue.text: Picked nose crudely after church

indicators.note: says the nose part comes after the church part
crudely means roughly made, so the letters of nose are roughly reshuffled

explanation.surface: Someone rudely picked their nose after leaving church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked nose' reads as one act, but 'Picked' is the definition and 'nose' is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Chosen and picked are synonyms meaning selected.

clue.text: Bunion? Not something a tennis player wants to hear

definitions.meaning: jokingly, a bunion is a fault in the foot

definitions.text: Not something a tennis player wants to hear
definitions.meaning: called when a server steps on or over the baseline

explanation.surface: A painful toe problem, which a tennis player hates to hear called.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, a foot fault is a service error; read literally it is a defect of the foot, like a bunion.

clue.text: Painter from German city one ignored

indicators.note: ignored means left out, so the letter for one is dropped from the city

parts.note: Munich is the Bavarian capital
I, the Roman numeral, stands for one

explanation.surface: An artist comes from a German city, one that has been overlooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Edvard Munch was the Norwegian painter of The Scream.

clue.text: Cat stole cook's stuffing on the way back

indicators.note: the run of letters is read from right to left
the answer is the stuffing inside these words, held within them

explanation.surface: A cat swiped the cook's stuffing while heading home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuffing' picks TOLECO out of 'stole cook's'; 'on the way back' turns it round. 'stuffing' looks like food, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a wild cat of the Americas, so it is an example of a cat.

clue.text: Funny smell by soldiers beginning to offend us

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: the beginning of the next word means its first letter only

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An amusing odour from the troops starts to offend the rest of us.
explanation.walkthrough: HUM as a noun for a pong is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Humorous means amusing or comic, a synonym for funny.

clue.text: Not in a fantastic state

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or wild, so these letters are wildly rearranged

explanation.surface: Not living in a wonderful condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' looks like a condition, as in a fine state, but it means a country.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation is a country or political state.

clue.text: Lifting catch, refuse to restrict Charlie's movement

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting raises the word upwards, so it is read bottom to top

parts.note: to net a fish is to catch it

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so the refusal word encloses the letter for Charlie

parts.note: deny means refuse
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Raising a catch while refusing to limit Charlie's moves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refuse' looks like rubbish but is the verb. A tendency is a faction within a political movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A tendency can be a faction or group within a political movement, as in the Militant Tendency.

clue.text: Beers mother gets in tin for trader

indicators.note: says the beers and mother go inside the tin

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
ales are beers
ma is a familiar word for mother

explanation.surface: Mum puts beer in a can for a merchant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tin' looks like a can in the surface but stands for its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A salesman sells goods, so he is a trader.

clue.text: Doctor able to make a speech very detailed

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters of able are rearranged

parts.note: orate means to make a formal speech

explanation.surface: A physician is able to give a highly detailed lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' rearranges ABLE to ELAB. It looks like a noun, a medic, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaborate means intricate, worked out with great care and detail.

clue.text: Period Toynbee regularly covers? On the contrary, this is prehistoric

indicators.note: the clue first says the Toynbee letters cover the period, then reverses it, so the period word encloses them

parts.note: a stage is a period or phase of development

indicators.note: regularly means picking letters at even intervals, here the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: A query whether a historian's era is covered by Toynbee, the historian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' reverses 'covers', so the period encloses the Toynbee letters. Arnold Toynbee was a British historian, which feeds the misleading surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stone Age was the earliest prehistoric era, before metal tools; as a modifier it means prehistoric or primitive.

clue.text: Study island's building material

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
Crete is the Greek island

explanation.surface: Examine what an island uses for construction.
explanation.definitionFit: Concrete is a mix of cement, sand and gravel used in construction.

clue.text: Tom maybe tense on top of large English farm animals

indicators.note: in a down clue being on top means coming first, before the letters that follow

parts.note: a tom is a male cat, given as an example
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
L is the clothing size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Tom, perhaps nervous, stands over large English livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom maybe' looks like a man's name; a tom is a male cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle are cows and bulls kept on farms as livestock.

clue.text: Large snake — run!

parts.note: L is the clothing size abbreviation for large
an adder is a venomous snake

explanation.surface: An alarm call warning of a big snake, telling everyone to flee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run' looks like a command to flee, but it is a noun: a ladder is a run in tights or stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a ladder is a vertical line of unravelled stitches in hosiery, also called a run.

clue.text: Repair robe after the Queen's upset

indicators.note: says the robe part comes after the Queen part
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher
a dress is a robe or gown

explanation.surface: Mending a gown after Her Majesty has been distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like distress but in a down clue it turns the royal letters upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To redress a wrong or imbalance is to set it right, to repair or remedy it.

clue.text: Dealing with Turkey by scoffing

parts.note: TR is the international vehicle registration code for Turkey
to scoff is British slang for eating greedily

explanation.surface: Handling the turkey by wolfing it down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turkey' looks like the festive bird but is the country.
explanation.definitionFit: To treat a matter or a patient is to deal with it, so treating means dealing with.

clue.text: Art gallery frames second preference

indicators.note: framing a picture means surrounding it, so the gallery word encloses the other letter

parts.note: the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: A gallery hangs a second picture by preference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frames' puts S inside TATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste for something is a liking or preference for it.

clue.text: In favour of first of changes editor made

parts.note: for means in favour of, as in the motion was carried with ten for

indicators.note: the first of a word means just its opening letter

explanation.surface: An editor backed the first round of changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' is the definition in the sense of compelled, as in made to resign.
explanation.definitionFit: Forced and made are synonyms meaning compelled, as in she was forced or made to go.

clue.text: Constant pain for Arsenal?

parts.note: C is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light
an ache is a pain

explanation.surface: A long-suffering football fan describes supporting Arsenal as a continual pain.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal is a London football club, which the capital disguises; here it is a store of weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: A cache is a hidden store, especially of weapons, so it is an arsenal.

clue.text: Underwear finally dropped, producing gasp

indicators.note: the final letter of the underwear word is dropped

parts.note: pants are underpants, underwear in British usage

explanation.surface: Someone's knickers fall down, causing a sharp intake of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain pants means underpants, not trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: To pant is to breathe in short quick gasps.

clue.text: Wants lazy son to go to the back

indicators.note: the letter for son is moved from the front to the end of the word

parts.note: slack means lazy or careless

explanation.surface: A parent wants an idle boy sent to the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go to the back' moves S from the front of SLACK to its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacks and wants are synonyms in the sense of being without, as in the room wants light.

clue.text: Central character in Wimbledon can have a wild fall

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters are thrown into a new order
the central character of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A player at Wimbledon takes a dramatic tumble on court.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of Wimbledon, L, joins CANHAVE, and 'wild' rearranges them into VALANCHE, after the A the clue gives as written.
explanation.definitionFit: An avalanche is a sudden fall of snow, ice or rock down a mountainside.

clue.text: Somehow cleverest hens not caught yet

indicators.note: somehow says the letters end up in some new arrangement
not caught means the letter for caught is struck out of the fodder

parts.note: anagram fodder once one letter is removed
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: The smartest chickens have evaded capture so far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes C from CLEVERESTHENS, and the anagram signal at the front rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevertheless and yet are both conjunctions meaning in spite of that, however.
